question: How reliable is the Gospel of Thomas?
subtitle: Dating, Thomas 114, and what we don't defend
aliases: is the Gospel of Thomas real
why isn't Thomas in the Bible
finding: Thomas is a real, ancient, independently circulating collection of 114 Jesus sayings with no narrative, no passion, no atonement and no apocalypse, and the honest claim about it is narrower than our own notes have sometimes made. The defensible position is layered: a kernel of early sayings inside a collection whose received form is late and accretive. The mainstream dating of the collection is c. 140 CE; the 50-70 date is a real minority position. DeConick's rolling-corpus model is the most defensible frame. So we use Thomas as corroboration where it parallels Synoptic material, as evidence about a documented early community where it stands alone, and never as a standalone proof. It contains sayings we don't defend and would not read aloud, and we name them. Subtract Thomas entirely and every argument in this collection still stands on the red text.
oneLiners: Mainstream dating is around 140. A real minority of specialists argue 50 to 70. We'll argue the layered model, and we'll tell you which layer we're standing on.
Whether Thomas is early or late, it proves a Christian community transmitted Jesus with no cross, no blood and no judgment day. One of those two conclusions is true, and both help us.
Thomas 114 is ugly and we don't defend it. It's the last saying, appended after the one that reads like an ending. That's what a late addition looks like.
"Women are not worthy of life" is Peter's line. Jesus's answer is that she stays.
Thomas has no love-of-enemies command. That's why our love argument comes from the red text and not from Thomas.
Nobody knows what Saying 7 means. I'm not going to pretend I do.
doNotSay: "Many scholars date Thomas to 50-70." A minority of specialists do; the collection as received is later. Say which layer you're standing on.
"No cross in Thomas." Thomas 55 has cross-bearing as the cost of following. Say: no passion narrative, no crucifixion account, no atonement theology, no blood.
Don't improvise an interpretation of Thomas 7 under pressure. There is no scholarly consensus.
Don't use Thomas for the love-is-the-law argument. It has in-group love (25) and no love of enemies or neighbor. Thomas supplies the epistemology; the Synoptics supply the ethics.

boardLabels.against: THE UGLY SAYINGS · READ THESE FIRST

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 3 and 113
sources.note: Set against Luke 17:20-21, two source streams agree on the kingdom's location and timing. That holds even on a 140 CE dating, because the point is attestation across streams, not Thomas's priority. The strongest use.
The Synoptic half of the parallel.

sources.tier: Thomas · Lambdin · against every later orthodoxy
sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 12
sources.note: No priesthood, no church, no Peter-gets-the-keys; the authority goes to James. Nobody invents that in 140 CE.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 70 and 1
sources.note: Whatever its date, Thomas documents a community that transmitted Jesus as a wisdom teacher whose answer to death was recognition: no cross-as-payment, no blood, no judgment day, no bishop. Early: a window onto pre-Pauline tradition. Late: proof the canonical process excluded them. Never let it become "prove Thomas is early."

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 9, the Sower without the allegory
sources.note: Mark 4:13-20 appends an allegorical interpretation; Thomas 9 has none. Patterson catalogued this pattern across the shared material. If Thomas were copying finished gospels, the consistent stripping of their editorial work needs an explanation. Plus: no passion at all, and roughly 37 of 114 with Q parallels.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 22
sources.phrase: make the male and the female one and the same
sources.note: "So that the male not be male nor the female." The dissolution of gender as a category. Saying 114 is a cruder, later restatement in the hierarchical idiom of its culture. An explanation, not an excuse.

sources.tier: Thomas · Lambdin · we don't defend it
sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 114
sources.note: Read it out loud yourself, first. The strongest candidate in the collection for a late accretion: last saying, appended after 113 which reads like a closing, in the ascetic idiom of the latest layer. "Women are not worthy of life" is Peter's line; Jesus's reply overrules the exclusion, and Mary stays. The same tool that handles 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 handles this: identify the layer, date it, don't attribute it to the center.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 56, 80, 87, 112, 29
sources.note: "Gnostic world-hatred." Concede the cluster: second-century Syrian ascetic milieu (Gathercole), accretion on the layered model. But read them: having understood the world you are "superior to" it, a knowledge claim, in a collection that says the kingdom is spread out upon the earth. And "whoever loves their life loses it" (John 12:25), "hate father and mother" (Luke 14:26), Romans 7-8 are canonical and harsher.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 7, the lion
sources.note: Nobody knows what it means. "That one's genuinely obscure" is a stronger answer than a guess, and it buys credibility for everything else.

sources.tier: Thomas · Lambdin · the most substantive criticism
sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 25, the only love command
sources.phrase: Love your brother like your soul
sources.note: "Thomas has no love-of-enemies and no love-of-neighbor." Verified. In-group love only; 101 requires hating father and mother. So the division of labor: Thomas supplies the epistemology, the Synoptics the ethics. The love case stands on Mark 12:29-31, Matthew 5:43-48, Luke 6:27-36, Matthew 25, John 13:34-35, Leviticus 19:18 and Didache 1-2.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 55
sources.note: Cross-bearing as the cost of following (Matthew 10:38; Luke 14:27), not the crucifixion as atonement. Make the precise claim and it's airtight.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 28
sources.phrase: I found all of them intoxicated
sources.note: "Thomas is a Gnostic gospel." Thomas has no demiurge, archons, Sophia myth, aeons or cosmogony. It exalts James, blesses the poor, debates circumcision in Jewish terms, and circulated in Greek at Oxyrhynchus. Concede what's real: 28 is a revealer-descent saying and the monachos material (16, 49, 75) has proto-Gnostic affinities, in the later layer. A wisdom collection with proto-Gnostic accretions.

sources.title: Nag Hammadi Codex II (c. 340, Coptic); P.Oxy. 1, 654, 655 (Greek, c. 130-250)
sources.note: Our earliest physical fragment is c. 200 CE and the only complete text is a fourth-century Coptic translation. Concede that first. Then: the Greek fragments prove Thomas circulated in Greek in Egypt before the Coptic, and differ from it in minor ways, which is direct manuscript evidence that the collection moved and grew in transmission.

sources.tier: the dating debate · scholarship, in copyright
sources.title: Goodacre (2012), Gathercole (2014) vs. Koester, Patterson, Crossan; DeConick (2005) in the middle
sources.note: Goodacre's argument is serious and partially correct: concede the Synoptic fingerprints in some sayings. His evidence is saying-by-saying and his conclusion collection-wide, which is what the rolling-corpus model predicts. Secondary orality is a real mechanism (Dunn). And the hole stays open: if Thomas read all three Synoptics, the total absence of the passion and the James appointment are unexplained. We cannot prove independence and don't claim to; genuinely contested is enough for corroborative use.

sources.title: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 2.9, the Gospel to the Hebrews
sources.phrase: He that wonders shall reign, and he that has reigned shall rest
sources.note: Thomas 2's saying, quoted about 200 from another gospel by name, so it circulated outside Thomas. The Coptic Thomas has no "rest" (that step is in the Greek P.Oxy. 654, not held); the 5.14 form names no source.

sources.title: Luke 16:13 // Matthew 6:24, the case for Q in one verse
sources.phrase: ουδεις οικετης δυναται δυσιν κυριοις δουλευειν
sources.note: Matthew 6:24 has the same 27 Greek words in the same order, lacking only οικετης. Agreement this close is what the Q hypothesis explains.
